content: Eczema is a chronic inflammatory skin condition that is commonly associated with other atopic conditions, such as asthma. Leukotriene receptor antagonists (LTRAs), which are known to reduce the need for corticosteroids in asthma management, have been proposed as a potential treatment for eczema. However, their efficacy in eczema remains uncertain. Current topical treatments for eczema are often poorly tolerated, and systemic therapies are limited by their side effects, prompting the need to explore alternative treatments. The objective of this review was to evaluate the potential benefits and harms of LTRAs in the treatment of eczema. A comprehensive search of multiple databases and trial registries up to September 2017 was conducted, including the Cochrane Skin Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and the GREAT database. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing LTRAs, either alone or in combination with other treatments, to placebo or conventional therapies for eczema in both acute and chronic phases were included. The primary outcomes assessed were changes in disease severity, long-term symptom control, and adverse effects. Secondary outcomes included changes in corticosteroid use, pruritus reduction, quality of life, and emollient requirements. The quality of evidence for each outcome was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Only five studies, involving a total of 202 participants, met the inclusion criteria. All studies investigated oral montelukast, and no trials assessed other LTRAs. Treatment durations ranged from four to eight weeks, with outcomes measured at the end of treatment, limiting the findings to short-term effects (less than three months). Montelukast was administered at a dose of 10 mg for adults (aged 14 years and older) and 5 mg for children (aged 6 to 14 years). Four studies included participants with moderate-to-severe eczema, while one study focused on moderate eczema. The studies were conducted in Europe and Bangladesh, with two being industry-funded. Comparators included placebo in three studies and conventional treatments (antihistamines and topical corticosteroids, with oral antibiotics in one study) in two studies. The methodological quality of the included studies was variable. Four studies did not adequately describe their randomisation or allocation concealment methods, leading to an unclear risk of selection bias. Only one study was judged to have a low risk of performance and detection bias. However, all studies were considered to have a low risk of attrition and reporting bias. The review found no evidence of a significant difference in disease severity between montelukast (10 mg) and placebo for moderate-to-severe eczema in the short term. Disease severity was assessed using the modified EASI (Eczema Area and Severity Index) and SASSAD (Six Area, Six Sign Atopic Dermatitis) scores. The standardised mean difference was 0.29, favoring montelukast, but the confidence interval (-0.23 to 0.81) included no effect, and the evidence was of low quality. When montelukast was compared to conventional treatment in one study, the mean improvement in disease severity (measured by the SCORAD index) was greater in the montelukast group (mean difference 10.57, 95% CI 4.58 to 16.56). However, another study found no significant difference between montelukast and conventional treatment (mean improvement of 25.2 points with montelukast versus 23.9 points with conventional treatment). The quality of evidence for this outcome was very low, making the results uncertain. Adverse events were reported in all studies. Four studies (136 participants) reported no adverse events. In one study of 58 participants, two adverse events (one case of septicaemia and one case of dizziness) occurred in the montelukast group, leading to study withdrawal, but it was unclear whether these events were related to the medication. Mild side effects, such as headache and gastrointestinal disturbances, were reported but were evenly distributed between the montelukast and placebo groups. The quality of evidence for adverse events was low. No studies specifically evaluated the impact of montelukast on emollient requirements or quality of life. One study assessed pruritus improvement and topical corticosteroid use after eight weeks of treatment and found no significant differences between montelukast and placebo. The evidence for these outcomes was of low quality. In conclusion, the findings of this review are limited to montelukast and do not provide evidence to support the use of LTRAs as an effective treatment for eczema. The quality of the available evidence was low to very low, and some important outcomes, such as long-term symptom control, were not addressed. The studies included only participants with moderate-to-severe eczema, primarily adults, and had small sample sizes. Further large-scale RCTs with longer treatment durations, including participants with varying severities of eczema, are needed to evaluate the potential role of LTRAs, particularly in the maintenance of eczema.
